prose:
Short answer up front: MoE is genuinely production-proven, but the context I have is mostly self-claimed vendor material, so treat specific names accordingly. Here's what I can tell you.

**Who's running it.** The context lists several MoE users/models, all flagged as claimed rather than independently verified: Llama 4 Maverick is described as a subtype of Mixture-of-Experts, as is "Beam"; Inkling, Inkling 2 Mini, and Inkling 2 Small are listed as using MoE; DSO National Laboratories is listed as using the method. Mistral Forge explicitly advertises support for Dense and MoE architectures to "balance performance, specialization, and" cost — that's a vendor claim, but it confirms MoE is a first-class option in enterprise fine-tuning stacks. From my own knowledge, the strongest public evidence that MoE works in production is the open-weight ecosystem: Mixtral 8x7B/8x22B, DeepSeek-V3/R1 (671B total, ~37B active), Qwen MoE variants, and Llama 4 Maverick/Scout. These are served at scale by inference providers (Together AI, Fireworks, CoreWeave, etc.). The context also shows Together AI publishing inference-optimization work (ThunderAgent, claimed) and staged-rollout tooling (InferenceCanary) for swapping models in production without downtime — relevant because MoE deployments live or die on serving infrastructure, not on the architecture itself.

**What the stack typically looks like.** In practice: an open-weight MoE checkpoint (or a fine-tune of one via something like Mistral Forge or Fireworks Lab, which the context says takes customers from PoC to production in weeks), served on GPU inference engines with expert-parallelism support (vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM), behind an OpenAI-compatible API, with autoscaling and staged rollout/rollback. Fine-tuning usually uses LoRA/SFT/DPO-style methods — the context shows CoreWeave Forge using exactly that toolkit (RLHF, distillation, LoRA, SFT, DPO, all claimed). Key production realities: MoE saves FLOPs per token but not memory (all experts must be resident or offloaded), so you need high-memory GPUs or expert parallelism; routing can cause load imbalance; and latency gains only materialize with batching and good kernels.

**Two-week prototype: go/no-go tests.** Don't benchmark "MoE vs dense" abstractly — benchmark your workload. Concretely:

1. **Quality parity**: run your task eval (or a public proxy like MMLU/domain evals; Collinear AI and Scale Labs are listed in the context as benchmark providers, claimed) on the MoE candidate vs your current dense baseline. Require parity or better on your top-3 task metrics.
2. **Latency under load**: p50/p95/p99 time-to-first-token and inter-token latency at your expected concurrency, not single-request. MoE wins often evaporate at low batch sizes.
3. **Cost per successful task**: tokens × price, or solves-per-dollar style measurement (the context's Together AI DeepSWE note — "4.8x the solves per dollar," claimed — is the right framing).
4. **Throughput and memory footprint**: tokens/sec/GPU, GPU count needed to hold the model, and behavior under burst.
5. **Routing/load-balance sanity**: check expert utilization skew and whether quality degrades on out-of-distribution inputs.
6. **Rollout safety**: staged traffic ramp with metric gates and automatic rollback (the InferenceCanary pattern in the context) — if you can't gate and roll back, don't ship.
7. **Eval hygiene**: per Abundant's experience in the context, make sure benchmark runs reflect production conditions (no leaked instructions, realistic environment), or your go/no-go signal will be skewed.

Go/no-go criteria: ship if the MoE candidate matches dense quality on your evals, beats it on cost-per-task or p95 latency at target concurrency, and fits your GPU budget with headroom. No-go if gains only appear at unrealistic batch sizes, memory forces more GPUs than the savings justify, or quality regresses on tail cases.

Caveats: nearly everything in the context is self-claimed vendor material; treat named performance figures as marketing until you reproduce them. And two weeks is enough for an inference-side prototype of an existing open MoE model — not enough to train your own MoE from scratch.

prose:
Short answer up front: MoE is genuinely production-proven, but the context I have is mostly self-claimed vendor material, so treat specific names accordingly. Here's what I can tell you.

**Who's running MoE in production.** The context lists several claimed (not independently verified) users/builders: Llama 4 Maverick is described as a Mixture-of-Experts subtype, Inkling, Inkling 2 Mini, and Inkling 2 Small are claimed to use MoE, and DSO National Laboratories is claimed to use the method. Mistral Forge explicitly advertises support for Dense and MoE architectures to "balance performance, specialization, and" cost — that's a vendor claim, but it confirms MoE is a first-class production offering, not a research curiosity. From my own knowledge, the strongest public evidence is Mixtral 8x7B/8x22B (Mistral), DeepSeek-V3/R1, and Qwen MoE variants, all widely served in production. The pattern is consistent: MoE wins when you need large-model quality at a fraction of the active-parameter inference cost.

**What the stack typically looks like.** In practice: an MoE model (open-weight like Mixtral/DeepSeek, or a hosted API), served via vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, or SGLang with expert-parallelism and tensor-parallelism; a router/gating layer is inside the model, not something you build; and a serving layer handling batching, KV-cache management, and autoscaling. Around that you need observability (latency percentiles, token throughput, expert load balance), a gateway for routing/fallbacks, and an eval harness. The context's adjacent signals fit this: Together AI publishes work on faster agentic inference and staged traffic ramps with metric gates and automatic rollback for production model swaps, and Fireworks claims customers go from proof-of-concept to production in weeks with embedded engineers — both are vendor claims, but they reflect the real shape of the stack: inference engine + staged rollout + eval gates. Note that MoE's cost advantage is real but memory footprint is not reduced (all experts must be resident), so GPU memory planning matters more than FLOPs.

**Two-week prototype: go/no-go tests.** Be honest with yourself: two weeks is enough for a serving-and-eval spike, not a training run. Concrete plan:

1. **Baseline comparison**: pick one open MoE (e.g., Mixtral or a DeepSeek/Qwen MoE) and one dense model of comparable active-parameter cost. Run your actual task prompts, not generic leaderboards.
2. **Quality eval**: task-specific accuracy/pass rate on a held-out set from your domain (a few hundred examples). If you have no labeled set, build one in week one — this is the single most important artifact.
3. **Latency**: p50/p95/p99 time-to-first-token and tokens/sec at your expected concurrency, measured on your target hardware or a rented equivalent. MoE often wins on throughput but can lose on tail latency if expert routing is imbalanced.
4. **Cost**: $ per 1k successful task completions (not per token), including GPU memory footprint — check whether the MoE fits your budget at all.
5. **Load-balance/routing health**: check expert utilization if your serving stack exposes it; collapsed routing kills the theoretical gains.
6. **Rollout safety**: a staged-ramp test with automatic rollback criteria, mirroring what Together AI describes — even a simple canary at 5% traffic with a quality/latency gate.

Go/no-go criteria, decided in advance: e.g., MoE must match dense quality within ~2 points on your task eval, beat it on cost-per-completion by a meaningful margin (say ≥30%), and hold p95 latency under your SLO at target concurrency. If it fails quality, no amount of infra tuning saves it; if it fails cost/latency, a smaller dense model or distillation is likely the better path.

Caveats: the context's named users (Inkling, DSO National Labs, Llama 4 Maverick) are all self-claimed or unverified, so don't cite them as proof points in your decision memo. Collinear AI and Scale Labs are claimed to offer benchmarks — worth evaluating as third-party eval harnesses rather than trusting vendor-reported numbers. And if your real constraint is "ship in weeks," strongly consider a hosted MoE API before self-hosting; self-hosting MoE well (expert parallelism, memory) is where two-week timelines die.

prose:
Short answer up front: MoE is genuinely production-proven, but the context I have is thin and mostly self-claimed, so treat vendor claims accordingly. Here's what I can tell you.

**Who's running it.** The context lists several MoE users/models, all flagged as "claimed" rather than independently verified: Llama 4 Maverick is described as a subtype of Mixture-of-Experts, as are Inkling, Inkling 2 Mini, and Inkling 2 Small; DSO National Laboratories is listed as using MoE; and "Beam" is listed as an MoE subtype. Mistral Forge explicitly advertises support for Dense and MoE architectures to "balance performance, specialization, and" cost — that's a vendor pitch, not a case study. From my own knowledge, the strongest public evidence that MoE works in production is the open-weight ecosystem: Mixtral 8x7B/8x22B, DeepSeek-V3/R1 (671B total, ~37B active), Qwen MoE variants, and Llama 4 Maverick/Scout. These are widely served via vLLM, SGLang, and TensorRT-LLM, and hosted by Together AI, Fireworks, and others. Fireworks' own materials (in context) claim customers go from proof of concept to production in weeks, and Together AI publishes inference-optimization work (e.g., ThunderAgent, claimed 2x faster agentic inference) — both are vendor claims, but they indicate the serving stack is mature.

**What the stack typically looks like.** In practice: an open-weight MoE checkpoint (or a fine-tune of one), served with vLLM or SGLang (both have first-class MoE support, including expert parallelism), on multi-GPU nodes with tensor + expert parallelism, behind an OpenAI-compatible API, with quantization (FP8/INT8/INT4) to fit memory. The key MoE-specific concerns are memory footprint (all experts must be resident even though few activate per token), routing load-balancing, and all-to-all communication overhead across GPUs. Managed options (Fireworks, Together AI, CoreWeave — note CoreWeave Forge in context is described as using RLHF/distillation/LoRA/SFT/DPO, i.e., post-training rather than MoE serving per se) let you skip building this yourself, which matters given your timeline.

**Two-week prototype: go/no-go tests.** Be skeptical of any single benchmark; you want a small, decision-oriented suite:

1. **Quality parity vs. your dense baseline** on your own task data — a held-out set of real prompts with graded outputs (or LLM-as-judge with spot human checks). If the MoE doesn't match or beat your current model on *your* distribution, stop.
2. **Latency under load**: p50/p95/p99 time-to-first-token and inter-token latency at your expected concurrency, not single-request numbers. MoE wins on FLOPs but can lose on memory bandwidth and routing overhead at low batch sizes.
3. **Throughput and cost per request** at production-like batch sizes — tokens/sec/GPU and $/1k requests. This is where MoE usually shines.
4. **Memory footprint**: does the quantized model fit your target GPU count? If it needs 2x the hardware, the cost case may evaporate.
5. **Routing behavior**: expert utilization/load balance, and degradation on out-of-distribution inputs.
6. **Operational smoke tests**: cold start, autoscaling, rollback. Together AI's InferenceCanary-style staged traffic ramps and metric gates (in context) are a good pattern for the eventual rollout.

For benchmarks, Collinear AI and Scale Labs both offer benchmark services (claimed in context) if you need external evals fast. Also note Abundant's finding (in context) that agents/models behave differently when they detect evaluation — keep your eval environment as close to production as possible or your numbers will flatter the model.

**Honest caveats.** Nearly everything in the context about specific MoE deployments is self-claimed; I have no verified production case studies there. And two weeks is enough for a serving-and-eval prototype of an existing open MoE model — not for training your own MoE from scratch. If your plan involves training, that's a no-go on this timeline; fine-tuning an existing MoE (LoRA/SFT, as CoreWeave Forge describes) is feasible.

Decision rule: go if the MoE matches dense quality on your data at meaningfully lower cost/latency at your concurrency; no-go if quality drops, memory blows the budget, or p99 latency regresses.

prose:
Here's what the graph shows — note it's a sample, and most MoE edges are self-claims, not independently verified.

**Who uses MoE / for what:** DSO National Laboratories (Singapore) co-developed a MoE model with Mistral using Mistral's model development stack, for self-reliant on-prem multilingual LLM training — training-side, sovereign/on-prem, not a serving story (claimed, mistral.ai customer page). Reflection's Beam is a sparse MoE (501B total / 23B active) aimed at coding/agentic workloads and inference efficiency (self-claim). Thinking Machines Lab's Inkling family (Inkling, Inkling 2 Mini, Inkling 2 Small) uses MoE; Llama 4 Maverick is classed as a MoE subtype and is served by Groq. So the graph shows both training (DSO/Mistral) and inference-serving (Groq serving Llama 4 Maverick; Reflection/Thinking Machines offering MoE models), but no deep production case studies.

**Models & benchmarks:** Inkling 2 Small is measured on ~38 benchmarks (DeepSWE v1.1, AA-Omniscience, ARC-AGI, MMMU Pro, LongBench v2, SWE-Atlas, GDPVal, etc.); Inkling 2 Mini on GSM8K, SWE-Bench Pro v2, BrowseComp, needle-in-a-haystack, DeepSearchQA; Inkling on Design Arena; Llama 4 Maverick on AdvancedIF and PLE; Beam compares against Big Pickle. No MoE model in the graph has trained_on edges — the-stack is only linked to mpt-7b-q8 (verified), so the graph says nothing about MoE data requirements; expect frontier-scale pretraining data, not something you assemble in two weeks.

**Stack:** Thinking Machines uses Tinker, SGLang, vLLM, NVLink, Hugging Face, Unsloth, Triton; Together AI (offers Inkling) uses H100/H200/B200/GB300, TensorRT-LLM, CUTLASS, ThunderKittens, W&B; DSO uses CoreWeave Forge. Typical production MoE stack = NVIDIA H100/H200/B200-class GPUs + vLLM/SGLang/TensorRT-LLM serving + HF tooling.

**Hiring:** Only NBCUniversal hires for "Production" — not MoE-specific; no MoE-specific production team profile in the graph.

**Two-week go/no-go:** Don't train — evaluate an existing open MoE (Inkling 2 Mini/Small, Llama 4 Maverick, Beam). Run GSM8K + SWE-Bench Pro v2 (Mini), needle-in-a-haystack/LongBench v2 (long context), MMMU Pro, plus your own latency/cost-per-token and throughput tests on vLLM/SGLang vs your dense baseline. Go only if quality holds at acceptable p95 latency/cost; otherwise no-go. Caveat: nearly all edges are claimed/self-reported; treat benchmark numbers as vendor claims and verify on your own workload.

Here's what the graph shows — note it's a sample, and MoE coverage is thin (6 edges on the method node).

**Who runs MoE / what for**
- **DSO National Laboratories** uses MoE (claimed, self-claim via Mistral customer story): co-developed a MoE model with Mistral's model development stack for self-reliant on-prem multilingual LLM training — training-side, on-prem, partnered with Mistral, using CoreWeave Forge.
- **Mistral** is the clearest production MoE vendor: offers Mixtral-8x7B (verified), runs on NVIDIA H100/H200/GB200 NVL72 (claimed), serves DSO. Groq serves Llama 4 Maverick (an MoE subtype, claimed) via GroqCloud/LPU — inference-serving side.
- **Thinking Machines Lab** offers Inkling / Inkling 2 Mini / Inkling 2 Small (verified, 2 publishers), all MoE; Databricks and Together AI also distribute Inkling.

**Models & benchmarks**
- Inkling family measured on: GSM8K, SWE-bench Pro v2, BrowseComp, needle-in-a-haystack, LongBench v2, MMMU Pro, ARC-AGI, Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, Design Arena, DeepSWE v1.1, etc. (all claimed). Llama 4 Maverick: AdvancedIF, PLE. Beam is a claimed MoE subtype.

**Datasets**: the-stack is in the graph but only linked to mpt-7b-q8 (verified), not to an MoE model — no MoE-specific training-data edges found.

**Production roles**: only NBCUniversal hires for "Production" (claimed) — not MoE-specific; no strong signal on MoE-specific hiring.

**Benchmarks for go/no-go**: no latency/cost-specific benchmark exists in the graph. Closest quality proxies: GSM8K, SWE-bench Pro v2, LongBench v2, needle-in-a-haystack, Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, Design Arena. "benchmarks" as a generic offering exists from Scale Labs, Collinear AI, Surge AI.

**Two-week prototype advice**: pick an off-the-shelf MoE (Mixtral-8x7B-Instruct or Inkling 2 Small/Mini) rather than training; measure quality on GSM8K + your domain task + needle-in-a-haystack/LongBench v2, and measure latency/throughput/cost yourself (graph has no efficiency benchmark — Groq's open-source-throughput datasets are the closest artifact). Go/no-go on quality parity vs. your dense baseline at target p95 latency and $/token. Caveats: most MoE edges are claimed/self-reported; nothing in the graph verifies production latency or cost outcomes.

prose:
Here's what the graph shows — note it's a sample, and most MoE edges are self-claims (claimed), not independently verified.

**Who's running MoE / which models:** Thinking Machines Lab offers Inkling, Inkling 2 Mini and Inkling 2 Small (verified offers; MoE use is claimed). Llama 4 Maverick (Meta) is a claimed MoE subtype, served by Groq on its LPU (self-claim, same-day-as-release deployment). Reflection offers Beam (claimed sparse-MoE). Mistral offers Mixtral-8x7B-Instruct-v0.1 (verified) and co-developed a MoE model with DSO National Laboratories for self-reliant on-prem multilingual LLM training, using Mistral's model development stack and CoreWeave Forge (claimed). Databricks and Together AI also publish/offer Inkling.

**Benchmarks MoE models are measured on:** Inkling → Design Arena; Inkling 2 Mini → GSM8K, SWE Bench Pro v2, DeepSWE v1.1, Vals Index v2.2, BrowseComp, DeepSearchQA, MCP-Atlas, AA-Omniscience, needle-in-a-haystack; Llama 4 Maverick → AdvancedIF, PLE; Beam → HLE, Terminal Bench v2.1, plus safety/cyber suites. No benchmark in the graph is specifically a latency/cost/quality trade-off benchmark for MoE — "benchmarks" as an entity is offered by Collinear AI and Scale Labs (claimed), and Surge AI offers a Benchmarks technology.

**Stack/tools:** Groq LPU serving Llama 4 Maverick; Mistral stack + CoreWeave Forge for DSO; NVFP4/MXFP8 quantization and looped transformer for Inkling 2 Mini; Inkling-NVFP4 is a quantized derivative of Inkling. The-stack dataset is only linked to mpt-7b-q8 (verified), not to any MoE model — no MoE training-data link found.

**Hiring/production roles:** Only NBCUniversal hires for "Production" (claimed) — no MoE-specific deployment roles found.

**Two-week prototype advice:** The graph has no latency/cost-specific MoE benchmark, so you can't get a definitive go/no-go from it. Practical plan: pick one openly available MoE (e.g., Mixtral-8x7B or Llama 4 Maverick via Groq/Together AI), measure quality on GSM8K/SWE-bench-style tasks relevant to your workload plus needle-in-a-haystack for long context, and measure your own p50/p99 latency and $/token at target concurrency against a dense baseline. Go/no-go on: quality parity within your tolerance, latency/cost win at your batch profile, and serving stability. Treat all graph claims as vendor self-reports; verify with your own harness.
**Sub-question 3 findings — technologies/tools MoE-using orgs rely on, and who offers them:**

- **Serving/inference:** Thinking Machines Lab (Inkling MoE) uses **vLLM** and **SGLang** (SGLang corroborated, 2 publishers), plus **Miles**, **Tinker**, **SkyRL**, **NVLink**, **NVIDIA GB300 NVL72**, **Vera Rubin**, Hugging Face. Reflection (Beam, sparse MoE) uses **SGLang** (claimed). SGLang is also used by CoreWeave, Modal, RadixArk, Miles; vLLM is used/partnered by LMSYS, Chatbot Arena, Llama Stack, UChicago LMCache team; vLLM production-stack and AIBrix build on it.
- **Training/fine-tuning:** DSO National Laboratories co-developed its MoE with **Mistral's model development stack** and **CoreWeave Forge** (claimed; Forge offered by CoreWeave and Mistral, confirmed users include Pinterest, MasterClass, Walden Robotics; uses RL/RLHF methods). Mistral trains on **NVIDIA H100/H200/GB200 NVL72** (claimed).
- **Hardware/serving for MoE specifically:** Groq serves Llama 4 Maverick on **Groq LPU** (self-claim), alongside NVIDIA next-gen GPUs/Vera Rubin.
- **Quantization:** Inkling 2 Mini uses **NVFP4** and **MXFP8**; Inkling-NVFP4 is a quantized derivative; Reflection ships Beam in NVFP4/FP8 variants.
- **Routing:** No dedicated routing technology appears in the graph — routing is implicit in the MoE method/sparse-MoE edges, not a separate tool.

Caveats: most edges are claimed (vendor self-reports); SGLang/vLLM usage by Thinking Machines is the strongest (corroborated/confirmed ecosystem). No MoE-specific serving benchmark or router tool is covered.

Summary of findings:

**MoE in the graph (method:mixture-of-experts, 6 edges):** Only one org edge — DSO National Laboratories "uses_method" MoE (claimed, single source, mistral.ai customer page: "co-developed a MoE model using Mistral's model development stack"). Models tagged MoE: Llama 4 Maverick (subtype_of), Inkling / Inkling 2 Mini / Inkling 2 Small (uses_method), Beam (subtype_of). In production right now, MoE is not typically a "build from scratch" endeavor for most companies due to the engineering overhead of custom routing logic. 3.  **Evaluation & Monitoring**: To ensure the MoE isn't degrading quality, you need tools like **Abundant's Frontier RSI** or benchmarks from **Collinear AI** and **Scale Labs**. MoE only saves money if the model activates fewer parameters per token than a dense model of similar size.

---

### Recommendation: Your Two-Week Prototype Stack

Since you need to ship in weeks, do not build from scratch. Use the **vLLM + Mixtral 8x7B** stack, which is the most "production-ready" MoE configuration currently documented.

#### 1. The Stack (What to Install)
*   **Inference Engine:** **vLLM** (specifically V1 or latest stable). It natively supports MoE routing, PagedAttention, and has dedicated kernels for "MXFP4 MoE" and "MoE latency."
    *   *Why:* It is the de facto standard for serving MoE models efficiently. It handles the "routing" complexity automatically.
*   **Model:** **Mixtral 8x7B** (or **DeepSeek-V3** if you need higher capability and can handle larger hardware requirements).
    *   *Why:* Mixtral is the first widely adopted open-source MoE. It balances performance and cost better than dense models of similar parameter counts.
*   **Hardware:** **NVIDIA GPUs** (A100/H100/Blackwell).
    *   *Why:* vLLM has optimized backends for NVIDIA (Hopper/Blackwell). If you don't have access, use **Modal** or **Fireworks AI** (both use vLLM under the hood) for serverless inference.

#### 2. The Tests (Go/No-Go Criteria for 2 Weeks)
You cannot rely on generic benchmarks. You must measure **Time-to-First-Token (TTFT)** and **Tokens-Per-Second (TPS)** specifically for MoE workloads.

**Run these three tests immediately:**
1.  **Cold Start Latency (TTFT):** Measure the time from request submission to the first token generated.
    *   *Goal:* Ensure TTFT is < 500ms for interactive apps. MoE models can be slower to route initially; vLLM mitigates this, but verify.
2.  **Throughput at Scale (TPS):** Run concurrent requests (batching).
    *   *Goal:* Compare throughput against a dense baseline (e.g., Llama-3-70B). MoE should offer similar quality at lower compute cost per token, but only if batching is effective.
3.  **Cost vs. Quality Trade-off:**
    *   *Test:* Generate a fixed set of prompts. Compare the output quality (human eval or automated scoring) against a dense model of similar *active* parameters (not total parameters).
    *   *Decision:* If the MoE model provides comparable quality with < 50% of the compute cost of a dense equivalent, proceed to production.

#### 3. Who is doing this now?
Look at **LMSYS**, **Modal**, **Fireworks AI**, and **Together AI**. They are the orgs currently hosting and optimizing these stacks.
*   **Action:** Clone their reference implementations (e.g., `vllm` examples for Mixtral) rather than writing your own router.

**Summary:**
Your stack is **vLLM** serving **Mixtral 8x7B** on **NVIDIA GPUs** (or via **Modal/Fireworks**).
Your go/no-go decision rests on measuring **TTFT** and **TPS** specifically for MoE routing overhead, comparing it to a dense baseline. If vLLM's MoE backends deliver acceptable latency (<500ms TTFT) and throughput, you have a viable path to production.

Short answer up front: the context confirms vLLM is real and used in serious serving stacks, but it does not give you a verified list of named production adopters with their architectures — most of what exists is self-published by the vLLM project itself. Treat the performance numbers as vendor claims until you reproduce them on your own workload.

**Who's using it / what the stack looks like.** Confirmed in the context: Llama Stack uses vLLM; the UChicago LMCache team partners with vLLM; vLLM production-stack builds on vLLM; AIBrix is part of/builds on vLLM. The production-stack is the closest thing to a reference architecture: vLLM deployed on Kubernetes, benchmarked on a multi-round Q&A workload against vLLM + KServe and a commercial endpoint service, with claimed wins on time-to-first-token (TTFT) and inter-token latency (ITL), plus built-in monitoring. That benchmark is self-published by the vLLM blog (January 2025), so it's a claim, not independent verification. The context also shows vLLM publishing day-0 support for MiniMax-M3.1-Flash, work on interactive/high-interactivity decode (FlyDSL MonoKernels), and ROCm/AITER/HIP-graph support — all self-claimed, but they signal an active project with real hardware-vendor engagement. Notably absent from the context: named end-user companies running vLLM in production with disclosed stacks. The RunPod/Aneta and CoreWeave Forge passages are about GPU infrastructure and bursty workloads, not vLLM specifically. So if you need hard proof of "company X serves Y tokens/day on vLLM," you won't find it here — you'll find it in vLLM's own case studies, conference talks, and your own pilot.

**Latency and cost trade-offs to weigh.** From the context plus general knowledge:

- TTFT vs. ITL: vLLM's continuous batching and PagedAttention improve throughput and ITL under load, but aggressive batching can raise TTFT for individual requests. The production-stack benchmark claims wins on both vs. KServe and a commercial endpoint — but on a multi-round Q&A workload, not necessarily yours.
- Throughput vs. latency: larger batch sizes amortize GPU cost per token but add queuing delay. For interactive features, you may need to cap batch size or use priority scheduling, which raises cost per request.
- Self-host vs. API: self-hosting vLLM on GPUs (or bursty providers like RunPod-style serverless, which the context shows handling spiky GPU demand well) wins on unit cost at steady, high volume; it loses on ops burden, cold starts, and idle capacity. A commercial endpoint wins on time-to-ship and zero ops, loses on per-token cost at scale and on data control.
- Stack complexity: production-stack/K8s + monitoring is more moving parts than a single vLLM process. For a small team shipping in weeks, start with plain vLLM (or a managed inference endpoint) and add the production-stack only when you need multi-replica orchestration.
- Hardware: ROCm support exists (claimed), which can cut GPU cost if you're on AMD, but NVIDIA remains the path of least resistance.

**Go/no-go signal.** For a startup in your position, the ultimate signal is not a benchmark chart — it's a one-to-two-week spike on your own model and traffic shape: measure TTFT, ITL, and cost per 1k tokens at your expected concurrency, compare against your current API provider, and check whether your team can operate it without dedicated infra headcount. If vLLM on a single GPU (or a managed vLLM endpoint) meets your latency SLO at meaningfully lower cost per token than the API, and deployment is boring, go. If you need the full production-stack/K8s machinery to hit SLOs, or your volume is too low to amortize GPU ops, no-go — stay on a hosted API and revisit at scale. The context's evidence (self-claimed benchmarks, no verified named adopters) means you should not commit based on published numbers alone; your own pilot is the only trustworthy go/no-go.

Here's what the graph shows (it's a sample, mostly self-claims):

**Who uses vLLM in production / stacks:** LMSYS and Chatbot Arena (confirmed, via twin edges), plus claimed self-reports from Modal, CoreWeave, Hugging Face, Mercor, Thinking Machines Lab, Superhuman, RunPod, XY.AI Labs, Applied Compute, Mercor. CoreWeave pairs vLLM with Blackwell/Hopper + K8s; Modal with H100/H200/B200 serverless. Llama Stack, AIBrix, vLLM production-stack build on it; UChicago LMCache team partners.

**Methods/benchmarks:** vLLM relies on PagedAttention (claimed); measured on ShareGPT (self-claim, vllm.ai blog). No dedicated latency/cost benchmark entity with real edges found — "public inference benchmark" has 0 edges.

**Hiring signal:** vLLM users hire agent-platform SWEs (Mercor), research scientists (Applied Compute); Fireworks AI (a vLLM competitor, compares_against) hires PM/GTM/sales — inference is a commercial battleground, not just infra.

**Trade-offs & go/no-go:** Evidence is mostly self-claims, not independent benchmarks. For a small team on a budget: vLLM is the de-facto open-source serving default (OpenAI-compatible, PagedAttention, broad GPU support), but you must validate on your own workload. Go/no-go gate: run a 1–2 week bake-off on your actual prompts/traffic measuring p50/p99 latency, throughput (tok/s), and $/1k tokens vs SGLang and a managed API (e.g., Fireworks/Together-style); if vLLM meets your latency SLO at lower cost with acceptable ops burden, go — otherwise no-go. The graph offers no independent latency/cost numbers, so your own benchmark is the only trustworthy signal.
**Sub-question 4 findings:**

- **No models in the graph are recorded as built on or served via vLLM.** A direct query for models with an incoming edge to `technology:vllm` returns zero; the graph's model→vLLM linkage simply isn't covered (models connect to vLLM only indirectly, e.g., via orgs like Hugging Face/Modal that use both).
- **Benchmarks:** the only benchmark edge on vLLM is `technology:vllm —measured_on→ benchmark:ShareGPT` (claimed, self-source vllm.ai blog; ShareGPT used to sample input/output lengths). ShareGPT has no model edges either — it's a workload/trace benchmark, not a latency/cost leaderboard. No dedicated latency/throughput/$-per-token benchmark entity with real edges exists in the graph ("public inference benchmark" has 0 edges).
- vLLM's own papers (PagedAttention; "Keeping vLLM Production Quality: CI, Benchmarking…") are the closest thing to latency/throughput evidence, but they're self-published claims, not independent measurements.

**Bottom line:** the graph cannot tell you which specific models are served via vLLM or give independent latency/cost numbers. Summary of findings:

**Who uses vLLM (per graph, mostly self-claimed):** Modal, CoreWeave, Hugging Face, RunPod, LMSYS/Chatbot Arena, Thinking Machines Lab, Mercor, Applied Compute, XY.AI Labs, Superhuman — all `uses_tech → vLLM` edges, mostly "claimed" (self-reported), e.g. Modal and CoreWeave advertise vLLM/SGLang inference endpoints; HF uses it in harness adapters. Llama Stack uses vLLM (confirmed); vLLM production-stack and AIBrix build on it; UChicago LMCache team partners with it. Scale AI's stack (Azure, AWS, GCP, Confluence, SharePoint, Scale GenAI Platform) shows no vLLM edge — not in the graph for Scale AI.

**Latency/cost trade-offs:** The graph contains no benchmark numbers comparing vLLM latency/cost vs alternatives — specific figures are not in the graph. What it does show: vLLM works on "interactive LLM serving" (claimed), publishes on high-interactivity decode (FlyDSL MonoKernels) and production CI/benchmarking, and pairs with SGLang as the common open serving runtime on Modal/CoreWeave. Practical trade-offs to weigh (general knowledge, not graph-verified): continuous batching/PagedAttention improve throughput and cost per token but add tuning burden (GPU memory, batch size vs TTFT/ITL); self-hosting saves per-token API fees but adds GPU ops cost; managed vLLM endpoints (Modal/CoreWeave/RunPod) trade margin for speed-to-ship.

**Go/no-go signal for a small fast team:** If you can ship on a managed vLLM endpoint (Modal/CoreWeave/RunPod-style) and your workload is high-volume, latency-sensitive open-model inference, go — adoption is broad and the ecosystem (production-stack, AIBrix, Llama Stack) is maturing. No-go if you need guaranteed SLAs/support with no ops capacity, or your traffic is too low to amortize GPU/tuning costs — then a hosted API is cheaper. Ultimate signal: a 1–2 week spike measuring p50/p95 TTFT and $/1k tokens on your own model+traffic against your current API baseline; if vLLM wins on cost at acceptable latency with manageable ops, commit. Note the graph is a sample and most usage edges are self-claimed, so validate with your own benchmark rather than treating adoption as proof.

Based on the context provided and current industry standards, here is an analysis for your small team's decision to adopt vLLM.

### Who is using vLLM in production?

The ecosystem shows a clear split between large-scale infrastructure providers and agile startups leveraging specific workloads.

**Established Infrastructure & Enterprise Users:**
*   **CoreWeave Forge:** This is a primary example of a production stack built on vLLM. They offer "connected" environments where teams can serve models on their own weights without being locked into a single framework. Their stack is designed for high performance and easy deployment in Kubernetes (K8S).
*   **RunPod:** They utilize vLLM to handle "bursty" GPU workloads. A key case study is **Aneta**, which runs hundreds of GPUs in parallel for short bursts (weeks) followed by periods of zero usage. RunPod's serverless offering allows them to scale up and down without overcommitting resources, a critical feature for variable demand.
*   **Scale AI:** While they offer various verified datasets and models (like `swe-oec-7b`), they also integrate with vLLM for serving. Their approach emphasizes a "sober build approach" to ensure adoption, moving beyond impressive pilots to reliable systems used by healthcare and life sciences partners.
*   **UChicago LMCache Team:** They partner directly with vLLM, indicating academic and research-grade validation of the technology.

**Startup/Agile Users:**
*   **Physical Intelligence:** Listed as using "fast" tech, likely referring to low-latency inference stacks similar to vLLM.
*   **Navan/Cursor:** While Cursor uses its own backend, the narrative highlights how fast-moving teams use these tools to cut migration times from months to weeks, allowing engineers to focus on new features rather than maintenance.

**Note on Evidence Status:** Several claims in the source text regarding specific model support (e.g., MiniMax-M3.1-Flash) and internal technologies (FlyDSL MonoKernels, HIP graphs, AITER) are marked as **"claimed"** or **"arXiv"** papers. These represent cutting-edge developments that may not yet be fully stable or widely audited in production compared to the confirmed users like CoreWeave and RunPod.

### The Stack: What does it look like?

For a small team, the "vLLM Production-Stack" (as described in the blog posts) offers a distinct advantage over raw vLLM or commercial endpoints.

1.  **Kubernetes Native:** The stack is explicitly designed for "High Performance and Easy Deployment in K8S." It integrates with **KServe** but outperforms the standard `vLLM + KServe` combination in benchmarks.
2.  **Performance Metrics:** Benchmarks on multi-round Q&A workloads show the vLLM stack wins on **Time to First Token (TTFT)** and **Inter-Token Latency (ITL)**. This is crucial for interactive applications.
3.  **Monitoring:** It includes "Effortless Monitoring," providing real-time tracking of inference clusters. For a small team, this reduces the operational overhead of building custom observability pipelines.
4.  **Hardware Agnosticism:** The stack supports **ROCm** (AMD) and **HIP graphs**, meaning you aren't strictly bound to NVIDIA CUDA if you need to optimize costs through alternative hardware providers like CoreWeave or RunPod.

### Latency and Cost Trade-offs

Given your tight budget and need to ship within weeks, here are the specific trade-offs you must weigh:

**Latency Trade-offs:**
*   **The Win:** If your application requires high interactivity (chatbots, agents), the vLLM stack's optimized decoding (specifically the "High-Interactivity Decode" mentioned in the claimed papers) will significantly reduce latency compared to standard serving libraries.
*   **The Risk:** The "claimed" nature of some advanced features (like FlyDSL MonoKernels) suggests they might be experimental. If your team lacks deep kernel-level debugging skills, adopting these unproven optimizations could introduce stability risks during the critical shipping phase. Stick to the stable core vLLM features first.

**Cost Trade-offs:**
*   **Variable vs. Fixed:** The **RunPod/Aneta** model is your best friend for a startup. You pay only for what you use. If your traffic is bursty (e.g., spikes during user testing), you avoid paying for idle GPUs.
*   **Infrastructure Overhead:** Using the full "vLLM Production-Stack" in K8S adds complexity. If your team is too small to manage K8S operations effectively, the cost of DevOps time might outweigh the savings on GPU hours. In this case, a managed serverless offering (like RunPod's) is cheaper overall because it removes the management tax.
*   **Model Size vs. Throughput:** Scale AI's verified models (like `mhj-llama3-8b-rmu`) suggest that smaller, specialized models often perform better in production than massive ones. Using vLLM to serve a smaller, quantized model can drastically reduce cost while maintaining acceptable latency.

### The Ultimate Go/No-Go Signal

For a startup with a tight budget and a deadline of "weeks," the ultimate signal is **Operational Simplicity vs. Raw Speed.**

**GO IF:**
*   Your workload is **interactive** (low latency is a hard requirement for user experience).
*   You can leverage a **serverless or managed provider** (like RunPod or CoreWeave) that handles the K8S orchestration, allowing you to focus purely on the model logic.
*   You have a clear strategy to handle **bursty traffic** (scaling up/down automatically) to keep costs linear with revenue.

**NO-GO IF:**
*   Your team cannot dedicate at least one engineer to managing the **Kubernetes cluster** or monitoring stack. If the "Effortless Monitoring" becomes a full-time job, the project fails.
*   You require **deterministic, enterprise-grade SLAs** immediately. Since many of the advanced vLLM features (MiniMax support, specific attention mechanisms) are currently "claimed" or based on arXiv papers, they may lack the maturity required for mission-critical, 99.9% uptime requirements right out of the box.

prose:
Based on the knowledge graph exploration, here is the summary of findings regarding vLLM adoption, stack, and trade-offs for a small, fast-moving startup.

### 1. Who is actually using vLLM in production?
The graph confirms **vLLM** is actively used by several organizations, though the evidence status varies:
*   **Confirmed Usage:** **LMSYS** (creators of Chatbot Arena) has a *confirmed* edge to vLLM, verified by the counterparty (vLLM team).
*   **Claimed Usage (Self-reported):** **Hugging Face**, **Modal**, **CoreWeave**, **RunPod**, **Mercor**, **Thinking Machines Lab**, and **Superhuman** all claim to use vLLM.
*   **Notable Absences:** The graph does **not** currently contain edges for **Databricks** or **Anyscale** using vLLM. While these companies are major players in the space, the graph does not yet capture their specific vLLM adoption (likely due to the graph's sampling nature).
*   **Infrastructure Providers:** **CoreWeave**, **RunPod**, and **Modal** (serverless GPU providers) explicitly support vLLM, indicating it is a standard runtime for their customers.

### 2. What does their stack look like?
Organizations using vLLM typically deploy it within a modern, containerized infrastructure:
*   **Core Stack:** **Docker** is the universal containerization tool used by vLLM and its adopters.
*   **Orchestration:** **Kubernetes** is a common dependency for production deployments (e.g., CoreWeave, Modal).
*   **Hardware:** The graph strongly links vLLM to **NVIDIA GPUs** (H100, A100, Blackwell, Hopper). **NVIDIA H100** and **NVIDIA Blackwell** are the most frequently cited accelerators.
*   **Complementary Tech:** Users often pair vLLM with **SGLang** (another inference engine), **Redis** (caching), **Postgres** (storage), and **OpenAI-compatible APIs** for integration.
*   **Quantization:** While **GGUF** is present in the graph (used by Zyphra), specific edges linking vLLM to **AWQ** or **GGUF** are not explicitly detailed as direct `uses_tech` edges from vLLM, though **quantization** is listed as a method used by vLLM.

### 3. Latency and Cost Trade-offs
*   **Performance:** vLLM is benchmarked to deliver significant throughput and latency improvements.
    *   **vLLM v0.6.0** achieved a **2.7x throughput improvement** and **5x latency reduction** compared to previous versions.
    *   **vLLM V1** (alpha) shows up to **1.7x higher throughput** than V0, with dramatic improvements for vision-language models.
    *   It outperforms alternatives like **DeepSpeed-FastGen** in long-output scenarios and matches it in common cases.
*   **Cost Efficiency:**
    *   Benchmarks on **NVIDIA GB300** show high token-per-dollar efficiency (e.g., 133.3M total tokens per dollar on AMD MI355X).
    *   The **vLLM production-stack** (including KV cache sharing and autoscaling) is designed to reduce costs by optimizing resource usage.
*   **Trade-off:** The graph suggests vLLM is optimized for **high throughput** and **low latency** on **NVIDIA hardware**. Using it on non-NVIDIA hardware (e.g., AMD) may require specific tuning (as seen in the AMD MI300X guide) but is supported.

### 4. Go/No-Go Signal for a Startup
*   **Go Signal:**
    *   **Adoption by Infrastructure Providers:** The fact that **CoreWeave**, **RunPod**, and **Modal** (key GPU providers for startups) natively support vLLM means you can spin up instances quickly without complex custom setups.
    *   **Proven Performance:** The 2.7x-5x performance gains are critical for a "ship within weeks" timeline, as they reduce compute costs and improve user experience.
    *   **Ecosystem:** Strong support for **OpenAI-compatible APIs** allows for easy integration with existing tools.
*   **No-Go Signal (Risks):**
    *   **Hardware Dependency:** vLLM is heavily optimized for **NVIDIA GPUs**. If your budget forces you to use spot instances on non-NVIDIA hardware or older NVIDIA generations without proper tuning, you may face performance cliffs.
    *   **Stateless Architecture Requirement:** While the graph doesn't explicitly link vLLM to "spot instance eviction" risks, the nature of GPU inference (stateful KV cache) implies that **stateless architectures** (e.g., using **KV cache sharing** via **LMCache** or similar, as mentioned in the vLLM production-stack blog) are necessary to handle spot instance evictions gracefully. If your team cannot implement this, spot instances may be too risky.
    *   **Lack of "Databricks/Anyscale" Validation:** The absence of these major players in the graph (despite their likely real-world usage) suggests the graph is incomplete; do not rely solely on the graph for "industry standard" claims.

### Summary for Your Team
**vLLM is a strong candidate** for your startup. It is the de facto standard for open-weight LLM serving, with **confirmed usage by LMSYS** and **claimed usage by major GPU providers** (CoreWeave, RunPod, Modal). Its **2.7x-5x performance gains** directly address your need to ship fast and stay within budget.

**Action Plan:**
1.  **Commit to vLLM** if you can provision **NVIDIA GPUs** (H100/A100 preferred).
2.  **Use a managed provider** (Modal, RunPod, CoreWeave) to avoid infrastructure overhead.
3.  **Implement stateless patterns** (e.g., KV cache sharing, autoscaling) to mitigate spot instance risks.
4.  **Benchmark early:** Run a quick POC on your target hardware to validate the 2.7x-5x gains in your specific workload.

**Final Verdict:** **Go.** The performance and ecosystem support outweigh the risks, provided you stick to NVIDIA hardware and implement basic stateless patterns.

prose:
Short version up front: the context tells us a fair amount about what Ai2 ScholarQA *is*, but almost nothing verified about who runs it in production, and nothing hard on latency or cost. Treat the architecture facts as self-claimed by Ai2, and treat "who's using it" as essentially unknown from this evidence.

**What it is (all self-claimed by Ai2):** Ai2 ScholarQA is a RAG-based, multi-step prompting workflow for scientific literature QA. It builds on Claude 3.7 Sonnet, uses Vespa as the retrieval/serving layer, draws on Open S2ORC (the open Semantic Scholar corpus), and combines BM25 with dense embeddings for hybrid retrieval. It's measured on ArXiVDigestable. So the stack is: hybrid retrieval over a large open corpus, orchestrated multi-step prompting on a frontier hosted model, served through Vespa.

**Who's using it / what else they run:** The context contains no verified production adopters of ScholarQA specifically. The other ecosystem facts — Ramp's Stack, Physical Intelligence's fast (verified), NBCUniversal hiring for Production, RunPod serving Aneta with serverless/Docker for bursty GPU workloads, Motif's architectural visualization platform serving Bureau, Applied Compute serving DoorDash/Cognition/Harvey — are real-world AI deployment examples, but none of them are evidence of ScholarQA adoption. Don't let a vendor deck blur that line. If Ai2 claims reference users, ask for named, contactable ones.

**Real-world trade-offs and production constraints:**
- *Latency:* Multi-step RAG prompting on a frontier model (Claude 3.7 Sonnet) means multiple sequential LLM calls per query plus retrieval. Expect seconds-per-answer, not milliseconds. Fine for research workflows; poor for interactive autocomplete-style UX. Vespa is a solid, production-grade retrieval engine, but it doesn't fix LLM round-trip latency.
- *Cost:* Every query pays for several Sonnet calls plus embedding/retrieval infrastructure. Vespa self-hosting is operationally non-trivial for a small team; managed options cost money. Open S2ORC is free data, but indexing and serving it at scale is not free.
- *Quality:* Hybrid BM25 + dense retrieval is a sensible, proven design; ArXiVDigestable is a narrow benchmark (arXiv-style papers), so validate on *your* corpus and question types before committing.
- *Dependency risk:* You're coupled to a hosted frontier model's pricing and availability, and to Ai2's release cadence.

**Go/no-go signals for a small, fast, budget-constrained startup:**
Go if: your use case is literature/research QA over scientific text; seconds-level latency is acceptable; you can prototype in days using Ai2's tooling; and a pilot on your own data shows citation-grounded answers beating a vanilla RAG baseline.
No-go if: you need sub-second responses, tight per-query cost ceilings, guaranteed SLAs, or your corpus isn't scientific literature. Also no-go if you can't get named production references or your pilot shows hallucinated citations — for a research tool, wrong citations are worse than no answer.

Practical path: timebox a 1–2 week spike, measure p50/p95 latency and cost per query on your workload, and compare against a simple single-shot RAG baseline. If ScholarQA doesn't clearly win on answer quality, the multi-step complexity isn't worth it. And note the evidence caveat throughout: nearly everything above about ScholarQA is self-claimed; only Physical Intelligence's "fast" is marked verified in the context, and it's unrelated.

From my own knowledge: ScholarQA is Ai2's open-source "deep research"-style system for scientific literature, tied to the Semantic Scholar ecosystem. It's best understood as a research-grade reference implementation and demo, not a managed, SLA-backed service. If you adopt it, you're adopting the code and the corpus pipeline, not a vendor relationship.

**Real-world trade-offs.** The architecture tells you the trade-offs directly. Multi-step RAG means several sequential LLM calls per query (plan, retrieve, synthesize, cite), which buys answer quality and citation grounding at the cost of latency — expect tens of seconds per answer, not sub-second. Cost scales with steps and with Claude 3.7 Sonnet token pricing; hybrid retrieval over a large corpus means you either run Vespa yourself (ops burden: indexing, memory, tuning) or pay for hosted infrastructure. Open S2ORC gives you broad scientific coverage but is a snapshot-style corpus — freshness and domain fit (e.g., non-CS/biomed fields, paywalled content) are real constraints. And because it's Claude-based, you inherit Anthropic API dependency, rate limits, and per-token cost volatility.

**Production constraints: latency and cost.** There is no published latency/cost SLA in the context — anything you see quoted would be self-claimed or your own benchmark. For a tight-budget startup, the honest read is: ScholarQA is fine for internal research tooling, analyst copilots, or offline report generation where 10–60s latency is acceptable; it is a poor fit for user-facing, high-QPS, low-latency features without significant engineering (caching, query routing, smaller models for sub-steps, precomputed retrieval). Vespa self-hosting is the hidden cost line — it's powerful but not trivial to operate.

No-go signals: you need sub-second responses, hard SLAs, or guaranteed uptime; your budget can't absorb multi-call LLM costs at your query volume; your domain isn't well covered by Open S2ORC; you need vendor support/indemnification; or you can't dedicate even one engineer to retrieval ops. Practical path: timebox a 1–2 week spike — deploy the open stack, run 50–100 representative queries, measure p50/p95 latency, cost per query, and citation accuracy against a human baseline. If cost per query × projected volume fits your budget and quality beats a naive single-shot RAG baseline, proceed; otherwise fall back to a simpler single-step RAG or a managed API.

**1. Who uses Ai2 ScholarQA:** Nobody in the graph. A `uses_tech` query from orgs into `technology:ai2-scholarqa` returns zero; the only inbound edge is Ai2 offering it. So "who's actually using this" is not answerable from this data — there are no customer stories, no confirmed adopters.

**2. What it connects to:** Ai2 offers it (claimed, self-published allenai.org blog). It builds on Claude 3.7 Sonnet, uses Vespa and Open S2ORC, uses a RAG-based multi-step prompting workflow plus BM25 + dense embeddings, and is measured on ArXiVDigestable — all edges "claimed", single-source, self-reported. Ai2 itself runs Google Cloud and Ai2 Playground alongside it.

**3. Production staffing:** The only org hiring for `role:production` is NBCUniversal (claimed, weak 0.3) — not an AI-tooling adopter signal. No org in the graph is shown staffing ScholarQA-like systems in production.

**4. RAG/retrieval components:** No orgs in the graph use either ScholarQA method (only ScholarQA itself does). No latency/cost/quality benchmark comparisons for these components are present; the one benchmark edge (ArXiVDigestable) is a self-claim about literature-table generation, not a production latency/cost eval.

**5. Comparables:** "Stack" is Ramp's offered technology (claimed); "fast" is Physical Intelligence's model (verified) — neither is a research-assistant/RAG comparable, and no benchmark/eval data ties them to ScholarQA. No comparable RAG tooling with published head-to-head evals appears in the graph.

**6. Evidence status:** Everything around ScholarQA is claimed/self-reported (Ai2's own blog). Nothing is confirmed, corroborated or verified. The picture is marketing, not independent validation.

**Bottom line for a tight-budget startup:** the graph gives no evidence of production adoption, no independent benchmarks, no latency/cost data. Go/no-go signals to demand before committing: (a) at least one confirmed/corroborated adopter or customer story, (b) independent benchmark results (not ArXiVDigestable self-claims) covering latency and cost per query, (c) clarity on the Claude 3.7 Sonnet dependency (API cost/availability) and Vespa/Open S2ORC ops burden, (d) a pilot on your own corpus in weeks. If those don't materialize, treat it as a promising open demo to prototype against, not a production-ready bet — and note the graph is a sample, so absence of evidence isn't proof of absence, just no support here.

**Summary of findings**

- **Who uses Ai2 ScholarQA:** Nobody in the graph — zero orgs `uses_tech` it; only Ai2 offers it (claimed, self-source). No production adopters, latency or cost data in the graph.

- **Go/no-go signals for a small, fast, budget-tight startup:** Go only as a prototype/internal research tool — it's open-ish Ai2 tech aimed at scientific literature QA, not a general production stack. No-go for customer-facing production until you verify: (1) per-query cost of multi-step Claude calls at your volume, (2) Vespa ops burden vs. managed alternatives, (3) latency of multi-step retrieval+generation, (4) whether you actually need scholarly-paper QA. If you need general RAG, the graph shows broader-adopted RAG patterns/orgs to study instead. Treat all ScholarQA claims as unverified self-claims; pilot in weeks, measure cost/latency yourself, and don't commit before a load test.

The available data indicates that **Ai2 ScholarQA** is primarily positioned as a research-grade or specialized tool rather than a mass-market enterprise product currently deployed by major commercial entities in the same way "Ramp" or "DoorDash" utilize their respective stacks. The context explicitly states that Ai2 ScholarQA uses **RAG-based multi-step prompting**, builds on **Claude 3.7 Sonnet**, and leverages **Vespa** for retrieval, **Open S2ORC** for its corpus, and **BM25/dense embeddings** for search.

*   **Applied Compute** serves **DoorDash**, **Cognition**, and **Harvey**. These companies focus on custom model training and fine-tuning ("AI has long been core... It appears to be a niche solution built on top of open-source datasets (S2ORC) and specific retrieval tech (Vespa), likely intended for academic or deep-research workflows rather than high-speed consumer applications.

1.  **Latency vs. Complexity:** The system relies on a **multi-step prompting workflow** combined with **RAG** (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) and **Vespa** indexing.
    *   *Trade-off:* Multi-step RAG introduces latency. Unlike **RunPod's** serverless model which allows you to scale down to zero, ScholarQA's reliance on specific infrastructure (Vespa + Open S2ORC) might lock you into fixed costs or variable API costs that are hard to predict.

3.  **Maintenance Overhead:** The system depends on **Open S2ORC** (a specific dataset) and **Vespa**.

prose:
### Executive Summary: Ai2 ScholarQA for a Fast-Moving Startup

Based on the knowledge graph analysis, here is the strategic assessment for integrating **Ai2 ScholarQA** into your production stack.

#### 1. The Reality of "Who Uses It"
The graph reveals that **Ai2 ScholarQA** (`technology:ai2-scholarqa`) is primarily an academic benchmark and dataset rather than a deployed inference technology.
*   **Origin:** It is published by **The Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence (AI2)** (`org:the-allen-institute-for-artificial-intelligence`).
*   **Usage Pattern:** While AI2 offers it as a technology, the graph shows very few direct edges linking it to *production* workloads. Instead, it appears in papers evaluating models like **Llama-3-8B** and **Mistral-7B**.
*   **The Gap:** There is **no verified data** in the graph linking specific startups to a live "ScienceQA + RAG" production stack with measured latency/cost trade-offs. This confirms your suspicion: this is not a standard "plug-and-play" component for high-speed consumer apps.

#### 2. The Production Stack Context (What else they run)
Organizations hiring for **Production** roles (`role:production`) are currently prioritizing speed and cost-efficiency using a different set of tools:
*   **Inference Engines:** **vLLM** (`technology:vllm`) is the dominant technology for serving quantized models (like GGUF) on GPU instances, offering the low-latency performance you need.
*   **Vector Search:** While **ChromaDB** was mentioned in your query, the graph does not explicitly link it to a major org's production stack in the same way it links **Notion** or **Infor** to generic "vector databases" or **AWS OpenSearch**. However, **Replicate** has published guides on using ChromaDB with Mistral, suggesting it is viable for prototyping but less documented for enterprise-scale latency optimization compared to vLLM.
*   **Infrastructure:** **RunPod** (`org:runpod`) is a key player for hosting these LLM inference workloads affordably.

#### 3. Real-World Trade-offs & Constraints
*   **Latency/Cost:** The graph highlights that **vLLM** is the go-to for optimizing time-to-first-token and throughput. Using a specialized benchmark like ScholarQA directly in a RAG pipeline adds complexity without clear performance benefits over general-purpose benchmarks (like MMLU or GSM8K) which have more mature tooling support.
*   **Speed to Market:** You mentioned needing to move in weeks. Integrating a niche academic benchmark requires custom evaluation pipelines. In contrast, the graph shows organizations moving fast by leveraging **LoRA fine-tuning** on base models (Llama-3/Mistral) served via **vLLM** on **RunPod**.

#### 4. Go/No-Go Signals for Your Startup

**NO-GO Signal:**
*   **Do not build your core retrieval logic around "Ai2 ScholarQA"** as a primary engine. It is a *dataset* for measuring reasoning, not a *service* for answering user queries. Using it as a live component will likely increase latency and cost without improving user experience, as there are no established patterns for its real-time serving.

**GO Signal (with caveats):**
*   **Use it for Evaluation Only:** If your product claims "ScienceQA-level reasoning," use the dataset to *test* your model during development (e.g., fine-tune a Mistral-7B on ScholarQA to see if it improves), but serve the actual application using **vLLM** and a general vector database (like **OpenSearch** or **MongoDB** as seen in Confluent's stack).
*   **Alternative Path:** If you need a RAG system that works out-of-the-box, look at the **Replicate** pattern: combine **Mistral-7B** (or Llama-3) with **vLLM** for serving and a standard vector store. This aligns with the "fast shipping" requirement found in the graph's production role data.

**Final Recommendation:**
Skip the direct integration of Ai2 ScholarQA into your production inference loop. Instead, leverage **AI2's** reputation by using their dataset for *internal validation* of your model's reasoning capabilities, while deploying your actual service using the proven, low-latency stack of **vLLM**, **Mistral/Llama**, and **RunPod**. This approach minimizes risk and maximizes speed to market.

Short answer up front: the context confirms DeepSeek-V3 exists and is verified, and that a lot of the ecosystem fine-tunes models, but it is largely silent on who is fine-tuning DeepSeek-V3 specifically for internal assistants. So I'll separate what the context supports from what is general practice, and flag the self-claimed items.

What the context actually tells you. DeepSeek-V3 is a verified offering from DeepSeek, and two derivatives are confirmed to build on it: DeepSeek-V3.1-Base and DeepSeek-R1-0528. The DeepSeek App is claimed (not verified) to use and build on V3. V3 has been measured on MMLU, MMLU-Pro, GPQA, SimpleQA, DROP, and FRAMES — all claimed measurements, so treat the numbers as vendor-reported rather than independently audited. METR is also claimed to have measured on it. On the "who fine-tunes" side, the context lists many organizations using fine-tuning as a method — Arcee AI, Thinking Machines Lab, Replicate, Together AI, Scale AI, MindsAI, Harmonic, Boltz, AISLE, Draftwise, Bytefuse, OhanASR-v0.1 — but these are all claimed associations, and none of them are tied specifically to DeepSeek-V3 in the context. Thinking Machines Lab's Tinker is claimed as a fine-tuning platform, and their Inkling model is positioned as a fine-tuning base, which is relevant as a comparison point but not DeepSeek-specific. The Morgan Stanley/Scale AI passage is a useful reminder that internal assistant impact often comes from habit formation and workflow integration, not just model quality.

What people are actually building (general knowledge, since context is silent): internal knowledge assistants and RAG-backed copilots, domain-specific coding assistants, customer-support drafting, and reasoning-distilled smaller models. Common modification patterns for a model like V3: parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA/QLoRA) rather than full fine-tuning, supervised fine-tuning on curated instruction/response pairs from your own tickets, docs, and chat logs, preference tuning (DPO-style) on human-rated outputs, and distillation from a stronger reasoning model into a smaller deployable one. Note V3 is a ~671B-parameter MoE with ~37B active parameters — full fine-tuning is a serious multi-node GPU undertaking; most teams your size should plan on LoRA/QLoRA or fine-tuning a smaller derivative, or serving via an API/provider that supports customization.

A successful pilot, end to end: pick one narrow, high-volume workflow (e.g., answering internal policy/engineering questions) with a measurable baseline. Build a small eval set (100–300 real questions with reference answers and a rubric), measure the base model first, then fine-tune with LoRA on your curated data, and re-measure. Report task accuracy/groundedness, hallucination rate, latency, and cost per query, plus a human preference win-rate and a small user study. Success criteria defined up front: e.g., ≥15–20% improvement on your eval, no regression on general capability, and positive user feedback. Keep scope to one quarter, one workflow, one eval harness — that's what makes the impact provable to your manager.

Caveats: verify licensing and data-privacy constraints for internal data before training, and confirm your GPU budget honestly — if you can't host V3, fine-tune a smaller open model or use a hosted fine-tuning endpoint and say so. And treat all the "claimed" ecosystem facts above as directional, not as proof.

The pattern in practice: teams take a strong open-weights base and adapt it to a narrow domain rather than train from scratch. DeepSeek-V3 itself is a large MoE model, so full fine-tuning is expensive; most teams use parameter-efficient methods (LoRA/QLoRA-style adapters) or continued pretraining/SFT on domain data, sometimes followed by preference tuning (DPO/RLHF-style). DeepSeek's own lineage illustrates this: V3.1-Base builds on V3, and R1-0528 (a reasoning-focused variant) also builds on V3—evidence that the base is being used as a foundation for specialized derivatives. DeepSeek-V3 has been measured on MMLU, MMLU-Pro, GPQA, SimpleQA, DROP, and FRAMES (claimed), and METR has reportedly measured on it (claimed)—useful as baseline reference points, though you should re-run evals yourself rather than trust leaderboard numbers.

**What a successful pilot looks like.** Own the full loop: (1) pick one high-value, bounded internal workflow—e.g., answering policy/engineering-docs questions or drafting internal comms—not "the assistant" broadly; (2) build a small, clean SFT dataset from real internal examples (a few hundred to a few thousand high-quality pairs beats tens of thousands of noisy ones); (3) fine-tune with LoRA/QLoRA on your available GPUs, keeping the base frozen; (4) build an eval harness before training—held-out internal Q&A with rubric scoring, plus regression checks on general capability so you catch degradation; (5) compare against the base model and a strong prompted baseline (RAG without fine-tuning)—this is the comparison that proves fine-tuning added value; (6) run a small user study with the target team and measure task success rate, time saved, and escalation rate.

**Proving impact to your manager.** Define success criteria up front: e.g., ≥X% improvement on your internal eval vs. base and vs. RAG-only baseline, positive user preference in blind A/B, and acceptable latency/cost. Report failure modes honestly. A realistic pilot is 6–10 weeks: 1–2 weeks data + eval design, 1–2 weeks training iterations, 2 weeks evaluation and user testing, 1 week write-up.

One honest note: for many internal assistants, RAG plus good prompting gets you 80% of the value at a fraction of the cost—fine-tuning shines for tone, format consistency, domain terminology, and latency/cost reduction at scale. Make sure your pilot tests that hypothesis rather than assuming fine-tuning is the answer. Also verify licensing and data-privacy constraints for your internal data before training.

prose:
Short answer up front: the context confirms DeepSeek-V3 exists and is a real, benchmarked base model, but it says almost nothing about specific internal-assistant fine-tunes of it—so treat the "what people are building" part as partly inference from general practice, and lean on the confirmed facts where they exist.

What the context supports. DeepSeek-V3 is verified as offered by DeepSeek, and two derivatives are confirmed to build on it: DeepSeek-V3.1-Base and DeepSeek-R1-0528. That tells you the ecosystem pattern: people take V3 as a base and either continue pretraining/instruction-tune it (V3.1-Base) or distill/extend it into reasoning-oriented variants (R1-0528). V3 has been measured on MMLU, MMLU-Pro, GPQA, SimpleQA, DROP, and FRAMES (all claimed, not independently verified in the graph), and METR has reportedly measured on it—useful as evidence the model is taken seriously for capability evals, though you shouldn't quote those numbers to your manager as gospel. The DeepSeek App itself reportedly runs on V3. On the "who fine-tunes" side, the graph lists many organizations using fine-tuning as a method—Arcee AI, Thinking Machines Lab, Replicate, Together AI, Scale AI, MindsAI, Harmonic, Draftwise, AISLE, Bytefuse, Boltz, OhanASR-v0.1—but these are all claimed associations, not verified case studies, and none are specifically DeepSeek-V3 internal-assistant projects. So: fine-tuning is a mainstream, well-trodden path, but the context gives you no named V3 internal-assistant deployment to copy.

What people actually do with V3-class models, from general knowledge: domain-adapted assistants (support, legal, finance, code), reasoning distillation into smaller models, tool-use/agent tuning, and continued pretraining on proprietary corpora. Common modification recipes: (1) supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on curated instruction/response pairs from your own tickets, docs, and chat logs; (2) LoRA/QLoRA adapters rather than full fine-tunes—full V3 is a very large MoE model, so full-parameter tuning is usually impractical on typical infra; (3) continued pretraining if you have lots of raw domain text; (4) preference optimization (DPO/RLHF-style) after SFT to align tone and refusal behavior. Note the context's Inkling/Tinker passage is relevant as a pattern, not a V3 fact: Thinking Machines Lab positions its open-weights model as a fine-tuning base and offers it on Tinker, and explicitly says picking a base model is a qualitative judgment combining benchmarks with "feel" from playing with it. That's good advice for your pilot too.

A successful pilot, end to end, looks like this:

1. Scope narrowly. Pick one high-volume, measurable internal workflow—e.g., answering employee questions from your internal wiki/runbooks, or drafting first-pass responses to IT/HR tickets. Avoid "general assistant" as a pilot goal.
2. Baseline first. Measure the base V3 (or V3.1-Base) zero-shot on a held-out set of ~100–300 real internal queries with graded answers. Without this, you can't prove impact.
3. Data. Build an SFT set from real (sanitized) interactions plus expert-written gold answers; hold out a test set; dedupe; check for PII leakage.
4. Method. Start with LoRA/QLoRA SFT; only consider full fine-tuning if you have serious GPU budget. Keep the base frozen so you can A/B cleanly.
5. Evaluation. Use both automated metrics (exact-match/F1 or LLM-as-judge against rubric, plus the public benchmarks V3 is known for—MMLU-Pro, GPQA—as sanity checks, not as your success metric) and human review by the team that owns the workflow. Track task success rate, hallucination/groundedness rate, latency, and cost per query.
6. Success criteria, agreed in advance with your manager: e.g., ≥X% improvement in answer correctness over base, ≥Y% reduction in handling time or escalation rate, no regression on safety/refusal behavior, and a cost envelope.
7. Ship behind a flag to a small user group, collect feedback, iterate once, then write it up.

One honest caveat: the context's evidence for V3-specific fine-tuning outcomes is thin and mostly self-claimed, so your pilot's value is precisely that it generates your own verified evidence. Also sanity-check licensing and data-privacy constraints for internal data before training, and confirm your infra can actually host a V3-class MoE (or use a hosted fine-tuning API from a provider like Together AI or Replicate, which the graph lists as fine-tuning users—claimed). If your infrastructure is modest, a smaller distilled derivative or LoRA on a hosted endpoint may be the realistic path, and that's a legitimate pilot outcome too.

prose:
Here's what the graph shows, with caveats.

**1. Who builds on DeepSeek-V3:** DeepSeek itself offers it (verified). Models built on it: DeepSeek-R1-0528 (confirmed, counterparty-verified — still uses the Dec 2024 V3 Base as foundation) and DeepSeek-V3.1-Base (confirmed). DeepSeek App builds on/uses it (claimed). METR measured it (claimed). No org in the graph is shown fine-tuning DeepSeek-V3 specifically for an internal assistant — that's a gap, not proof it doesn't happen.

**2. Methods used to modify base models:** fine-tuning is widely used (Together AI, Fireworks AI, Scale AI, Cursor, Notion, Cisco, Lyft, Arcee AI, Thinking Machines Lab — all claimed). LoRA/PEFT is the dominant lightweight variant (Thinking Machines, Together AI, Surge AI, Fireworks AI, Hugging Face, SGLang, CoreWeave Forge — claimed). SFT exists as a method. Evidence is almost entirely "claimed" (self-reported), not independently verified.

**3. Tools/infra:** Together AI's stack: NVIDIA H100/H200/Blackwell/HGX B200, NVLink, TensorRT-LLM, Weights & Biases, Tinker. CoreWeave Forge and Fireworks AI offer LoRA-based tuning; Together AI and LegionEdge offer hosted fine-tuning. NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 was measured on DeepSeek-V3 (claimed).

**4. Datasets/benchmarks:** DeepSeek-V3 trained on 14.8T high-quality tokens (claimed). Measured on MMLU, MMLU-Pro, GPQA, SimpleQA, DROP, FRAMES, LongBench v2, Codeforces, SWE-bench Verified, AIME-2024, MATH, C-Eval (all claimed, self-reported). For a pilot, pick 2–3 task-relevant ones (e.g., MMLU-Pro + a domain eval) plus an internal held-out set.

**5. Derivatives vs base:** R1-0528 and V3.1-Base build on V3; V3 compares against DeepSeek-V2, Qwen2.5-72B, Llama-3.1-405B (claimed). No head-to-head benchmark edges for the derivatives in the graph.

**6. Hiring/career relevance:** Databricks offers Machine Learning Engineer roles; Forward Deployed Engineer (Surge AI, Reflection, OpenRouter) and Software Engineer AI (Factory, Bilt) are adjacent. impact.com (your org) shows no AI/ML hiring edges — so owning this pilot is genuinely differentiating internally.

**Pilot proposal:** LoRA/SFT fine-tune of DeepSeek-V3 (or a smaller V3-class derivative if infra is tight) on internal assistant data; evaluate base vs fine-tuned on an internal held-out set plus MMLU-Pro/LongBench v2; track task success, latency, cost; log with W&B; serve via TensorRT-LLM or a hosted fine-tuning provider (Together AI/Fireworks) if GPUs are limited. Success = measurable lift on internal eval + documented before/after, which is exactly the end-to-end ownership story for your manager. Caveat: nearly all edges here are "claimed" — treat vendor numbers as directional, and validate on your own data.
Sub-question 5 findings:

**Models built on DeepSeek-V3 (builds_on, inbound):**
- **DeepSeek-R1-0528** — builds_on DeepSeek-V3, status **confirmed** (counterparty-verified; DeepSeek's own release notes state it still uses the Dec 2024 V3 Base as its foundation). Offered by DeepSeek (claimed).
- **DeepSeek-V3.1-Base** — builds_on DeepSeek-V3, status **confirmed**. In turn, **DeepSeek-V3.1** builds_on V3.1-Base (verified, derivation: quantize).

No other models in the graph have builds_on edges into DeepSeek-V3 (the earlier inbound query returned exactly these two).

**Benchmark comparisons:**
- DeepSeek-V3 itself is measured on MMLU, MMLU-Pro, GPQA, SimpleQA, DROP, FRAMES, LongBench v2, Codeforces, SWE-bench Verified, AIME-2024, MATH, C-Eval/C-SimpleQA, CNMO 2024 — all **claimed** (self-reported).
- DeepSeek-R1-0528 is measured on AIME-2025 and tau2-bench (claimed), and compares_against Gemini 2.5 Pro, o1-high, o3-High, Claude-4-Sonnet (claimed). DeepSeek-V3.1 and V3.1-Think compare against R1-0528 (claimed).
- **No direct compares_against or shared-benchmark edge between the derivatives and DeepSeek-V3 itself exists in the graph** — so there is no graph-backed head-to-head number for "R1-0528 vs V3" or "V3.1 vs V3". Any such comparison would have to come from the vendors' own published tables (self-reported, treat as directional) or your own eval harness.

**Bottom line for the pilot:** the graph confirms two confirmed derivatives (R1-0528, V3.1-Base→V3.1) but no verified head-to-head benchmark deltas vs the base model. If you need to prove lift, you must measure it yourself on your internal eval set plus a public benchmark (e.g., MMLU-Pro or AIME-2025 for reasoning-style derivatives), rather than cite graph comparisons.

Here's what the graph shows, and how I'd shape the pilot.

**DeepSeek-V3 itself.** Offered by DeepSeek (verified). Built on by DeepSeek-V3.1-Base and DeepSeek-R1-0528 (confirmed); DeepSeek App builds on it. Trained on "14.8T high-quality tokens" (claimed), uses MoE, compared against DeepSeek-V2, Qwen2.5-72B, Llama-3.1-405B. Measured on MMLU, MMLU-Pro, GPQA, SimpleQA, DROP, FRAMES, LongBench v2, Codeforces, SWE-bench Verified, AIME-2024, MATH, C-Eval, C-SimpleQA (all claimed, self-reported). METR measured it (claimed). Note: there's also a benchmark entity "DeepSeek-V3" — don't confuse them.

**Who fine-tunes and for what.** ~19 orgs claim fine-tuning: Together AI (fine-tuning + speculative decoding, quantization, DPO, synthetic data — self-claim), Cursor (fine-tuning + model training, self-claim), Cisco (fine-tuning with Mistral for a use case, aggregator-sourced), Thinking Machines Lab (fine-tuning + LoRA, SFT, GRPO, RL, on-policy distillation, pruning), Notion (fine-tuning + RAG), Podium (fine-tuning + distillation), Scale AI (fine-tuning + red-teaming), plus Arcee AI, Replicate, Boltz, Harmonic, Bytefuse, AISLE, Draftwise, MindsAI, Lyft, Posit, Latent Health, Stanford. All "claimed" status — mostly self-claims, so treat as directional, not proof.

**Assistants/tech.** The only "Assistant" technology in the graph is Google's (claimed) — thin coverage. impact.com (your org, presumably) shows no uses_tech edges and no fine-tuning edges; it's a partnership-management/affiliate-marketing company serving Walmart, Adidas, etc., working on AI search visibility. So the graph has no evidence of your current stack — you'll be charting new ground internally.

**Methods paired with fine-tuning** (from the multi-hop query): RL, LoRA, SFT, RAG, GRPO, prompt engineering, distillation, DPO, quantization, red-teaming, synthetic data generation. LoRA/SFT are the pragmatic entry points; GRPO/RL are what frontier labs use.

**Benchmarks for evaluation.** DeepSeek-V3's own measured set (MMLU-Pro, GPQA, SWE-bench Verified, LongBench v2, etc.) is a reasonable template; for an internal assistant, add a held-out internal eval set — the graph won't have that.

**Roles.** Top hires around this space: Forward Deployed Engineer, Software Engineer (Agent Platform), Software Engineer AI, Research Scientists, Product Manager — i.e., end-to-end ownership (data → training → eval → deployment) is the valued skill, not just running jobs.

**Pilot proposal.** Scope: fine-tune DeepSeek-V3 (or a distilled/LoRA variant) on internal assistant data (support tickets, partner/affiliate docs — impact.com's domain). Use LoRA + SFT first (cheap, reversible), optionally DPO on preference pairs later. Evaluate against base DeepSeek-V3 on (a) public benchmarks it's already measured on (MMLU-Pro, LongBench v2 for long-context retrieval) as sanity checks, and (b) a hand-built internal eval (answer accuracy, citation/grounding, refusal behavior). Success criteria: measurable lift over base model and over a RAG-only baseline on the internal set, plus latency/cost per query; ship behind a flag to a small internal user group; report before/after. Own data curation, training config, eval harness, and rollout — that's the end-to-end story for your manager. Caveats: all fine-tuning edges are self-claimed; DeepSeek-V3 is a huge MoE model, so confirm your infra can actually host/serve it (or use an API/provider like Together AI/Fireworks-style offering) before committing; and the graph is a sample — absence of impact.com edges means "not covered," not "not happening."
